**Answer**

Lions (Panthera leo) and zebras (Equus quagga) belong to very different mammalian families—Felidae (carnivores) and Equidae (odd‑toed ungulates).  
Their most recent common ancestor is therefore not a modern animal but a **small, probably insectivorous mammal that lived in the late Cretaceous, roughly 90–100 million years ago**.  

That ancestor is the last common ancestor of the two major clades that give rise to today’s carnivores (Carnivora) and odd‑toed ungulates (Perissodactyla). In phylogenetic terms it sits at the base of the **Laurasiatheria** super‑clade, the group that contains most of the placental mammals that evolved on the northern supercontinent Laurasia.  

So, in short: the common ancestor of a lion and a zebra is a small, insect‑eating mammal from the late Cretaceous, the last shared ancestor of the lineages that led to modern carnivores and odd‑toed ungulates.
